name: Liraglutide
lead: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist made by Novo Nordisk and given by daily subcutaneous injection. Under the brand name Victoza it is used for type 2 diabetes, and at a higher strength as Saxenda it is used for chronic weight management; it is also available as a generic [1][16]. It was approved in the European Union in 2009 and in the United States in 2010 [1].

Its weight-loss effect in trials is smaller than that of the newer weekly drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide. Wikipedia describes liraglutide as less effective than standard-dose semaglutide for weight loss, and the STEP 8 trial compared the two directly [1][7]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it is discussed mostly as an older, shorter-acting alternative that some users prefer because the daily schedule lets them time doses [20].

The US label has a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents, and other labelled risks include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia with some other diabetes drugs, and acute kidney injury from volume depletion [16].

paras: Victoza is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in people aged ten and over with type 2 diabetes, and to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease [1][16]. Saxenda is indicated with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for long-term weight reduction in people aged twelve and over with obesity and a body weight above 60 kg, and in adults with overweight and a weight-related condition [1]. American Diabetes Association guidance cited by Wikipedia considers it a first-line option for people with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or obesity [1].

Appearance-focused users take liraglutide to lose body fat through appetite suppression. As with other GLP-1 drugs, it is not known to affect facial fat selectively; any facial change follows overall fat loss. Forum posters mention it as a cheaper or lower-intensity option than semaglutide, with some saying that peptide sites sell liraglutide [20][21].

In the SCALE trial, 3,731 people with obesity or overweight and no type 2 diabetes received liraglutide 3.0 mg or placebo for 56 weeks [8]. A separate SCALE Diabetes trial tested the same dose in people with type 2 diabetes [13], and a 3-year trial tested it in people with prediabetes for diabetes risk reduction and weight management [12]. In the head-to-head STEP 8 trial, weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg was compared with daily liraglutide 3.0 mg over 68 weeks [7]. Wikipedia states liraglutide led to greater weight loss than some earlier GLP analogues but less than standard-dose semaglutide [1].

A 2025 network meta-analysis of body composition found that liraglutide was the only GLP-1 agonist in that analysis to produce significant weight reduction without a significant reduction in lean mass, though the analysis was across heterogeneous trials [3]. Another randomized trial examined combining exercise with a GLP-1 agonist on metabolic syndrome and abdominal obesity [10]. A 2025 meta-analysis of GLP-1 drugs examined weight after discontinuation [4].

Common effects include nausea, dizziness, abdominal pain, injection-site pain and low blood sugar when combined with other glucose-lowering drugs. Gastrointestinal effects are strongest at the start of treatment and tend to subside [1]. Serious effects listed include angioedema, pancreatitis, gallbladder disease and kidney problems [1]. The label warns about thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents, which is a boxed warning, and says it is unknown whether liraglutide causes such tumors in humans [16]. Wikipedia notes that in clinical trials thyroid tumor rates were 1.3 versus 1.0 per 1,000 participant-years, with most cases having elevated calcitonin at baseline, and that the FDA required long-term monitoring in a cancer registry [1]. The label recommends not sharing pens between patients and says animal studies suggest possible fetal risk [16]. A 2025 meta-analysis assessed class-wide safety across 99,599 patients [5].

Liraglutide is an acylated GLP-1 analogue with 97 percent amino-acid sequence homology to human GLP-1(7-37). It activates the GLP-1 receptor, raising cyclic AMP in pancreatic beta cells and increasing insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent way [16]. A fatty-acid chain promotes albumin binding and gives a half-life of about 13 hours, allowing once-daily dosing [2][6]. Review literature describes how the discovery of GLP-1 and efforts to extend its short half-life led to liraglutide and then to semaglutide [6].

Novo Nordisk developed liraglutide after the discovery of GLP-1 and early efforts to extend its half-life; a 2019 review charts the discovery and development of liraglutide and, later, semaglutide [6]. The EU approved it in 2009 and the US in 2010 [1]. The LEADER trial reported cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes in 2016 and a renal-outcomes analysis followed in 2017 [9][15]. The SCALE program supported the weight-management product [8].

Liraglutide is mentioned less than semaglutide and tirzepatide. T Nation members describe using it for appetite control, getting it as Saxenda or from peptide sellers, and sometimes preferring it because of its shorter action [20][19][22]. One poster reports losing roughly 30 pounds and then regaining some after stopping [21], and another reports tiredness from low calorie intake and constant fullness [23]. Others mention insurance covering Victoza as a diabetes drug [18].

Liraglutide has an extensive randomized trial record. For weight, SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes, SCALE Diabetes, a 3-year prediabetes trial and STEP 8 (against semaglutide) are the main publications [8][13][12][7]. LEADER and a renal-outcomes analysis addressed cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in type 2 diabetes [9][15], LEAN tested liraglutide in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis [14], and a 2025 trial studied children aged 6 to under 12 with obesity [11]. A registered phase 2 study examined it in adolescents after sleeve gastrectomy [17]. No published trial has tested liraglutide for facial appearance.

timeline.event: SCALE trial of 3.0 mg for weight management published [8].

lore.intro: In T Nation and similar forums liraglutide is treated as the older, shorter-acting GLP-1 option, mentioned alongside semaglutide for appetite control and cutting [20][21][22].

claims.claim: Liraglutide's shorter action lets users dose around cravings.
claims.believers: One T Nation poster says they use both semaglutide and liraglutide and prefer liraglutide because they can take it when cravings hit [20].
claims.experts: The label and Wikipedia describe it as a once-daily injection with a half-life of about 13 hours; no trial has tested ad hoc timing for cravings [16][2].

claims.claim: It is milder and less potent than semaglutide.
claims.believers: Users contrast it with the stronger effect and side effects of semaglutide [20][21].
claims.experts: Trials and reviews report smaller average weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg, and STEP 8 compared them directly [1][7].

claims.believers: One poster lost about 30 lb and regained part of it in the following year off the drug [21].
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis of GLP-1 drugs examined weight after discontinuation and found regain [4].

claims.claim: Liraglutide spares muscle better than other GLP-1 drugs.
claims.believers: Posters discuss muscle retention as a reason for choosing among GLP-1 agents [23].
claims.experts: A 2025 network meta-analysis found liraglutide was the only agent in that analysis with significant weight loss and no significant lean mass loss, with caveats about trial heterogeneity [3].

claims.claim: Low calories plus constant fullness make training a chore.
claims.believers: A poster on Wegovy and liraglutide reports being tired almost all the time and finding training harder [23].
claims.experts: Label and trial adverse-event data list gastrointestinal effects; fatigue from calorie restriction was not the focus of the cited trials [16][8].

claims.claim: Peptide-site liraglutide is an equivalent substitute for prescribed Saxenda.
claims.believers: Users mention buying liraglutide from peptide sites at lower cost [20].
claims.experts: Trials and the label concern the manufacturer's prescription product, and no published study has tested peptide-site supplies [16][8].
